whatItDoes: Parses HTML table markup into structured JSON in the browser. Paste a <table> snippet, choose whether the first row is a header, and the tool converts rows and cells into an array of objects keyed by header text. Supports multiple tables in one document.
whyItExists: HTML tables on the web are convenient to read but awkward to consume as data. Converting them to JSON makes them usable in spreadsheets, scripts, and data pipelines without manual transcription or fragile scraping.
whoShouldUse: Data analysts harvesting data from the web, developers building scrapers or migrations, and anyone who wants table data as JSON for further processing.
useCases: Extract a pricing or comparison table from a page as JSON
Migrate legacy HTML tables into a modern data pipeline
Convert a document's tables into spreadsheet-ready objects
Verify how a scraper would interpret the rows and columns
instructions:

snippet) into the input
Toggle 'First row is header' depending on your table
Copy or download the resulting JSON
examples: A table with no header row → array of row arrays
Multiple <table> elements → one JSON object per table
Cells with numbers stay as strings by default; toggle numeric coercion to convert them
bestPractices: Mark the first row as header when it contains column titles
Use numeric coercion only when your data is consistently numeric
Test on a single table before processing a full page
Sanitize source HTML — never paste it into a live DOM unless you control it
commonMistakes: Mixing tables with different header structures in one document
Assuming all cells are numeric when some contain units or text
Forgetting that rowspan/colspan cells repeat in the output
Relying on HTML that has malformed or unclosed tags
faq: Does this handle rowspan and colspan? — Yes, spanning cells are expanded to fill their covered columns.
Can I parse multiple tables at once? — Yes, each top-level table becomes a separate JSON object.
Is the HTML executed? — No, it is parsed as data only, never rendered or executed.
Is anything uploaded? — No, all parsing happens locally in your browser.
